self_critique:
Overall assessment

The run found a small accepted gain over FM (+0.0026, from 0.6018 to 0.6044), but it generated little reusable causal knowledge. The main limitation was experimental design and observability rather than a lack of plausible ideas.

What the harness/policy did suboptimally

- Node 001 bundled architecture, BCE/BPR mixing, dropout, weight decay, LR schedule, recency weighting, and capacity changes. Its success cannot be attributed to any component, making subsequent search poorly grounded.
- Learning-curve instrumentation was inconsistent. Node 001 cited a peak at epoch 8, while later nodes said the parent curve was unavailable. Curves, selected checkpoints, and epoch-level metrics should have been inherited automatically.
- Nodes 002 and 003 had higher nominal scores (0.6047) than the accepted incumbent but were rejected. The journal does not expose paired variance, acceptance margins, seed counts, or rejection reasons, so it is impossible to tell whether these were noise, a multiple-testing safeguard, or a flawed gate.
- The policy moved too quickly across loss design, negative sampling, and an entirely new sequence model rather than exploiting the strongest branch with controlled ablations.
- Node 004 was an oversized, expensive package for a CPU-limited run. It combined sequence history, temporal/session features, auxiliary supervision, regularization search, and seed ensembling, again preventing attribution.
- Claimed improvements such as “approximately 0.0012” were not visibly calibrated from prior trials. These forecasts added confidence without evidence.
- Budget use was weak: the run stopped on max_hours after only five nodes, suggesting that large trials or repeated training consumed time without enough staged screening.

What I would change in the scaffold

- Enforce one substantive change per trial unless explicitly running a final synthesis experiment.
- Persist full per-epoch train/validation curves, checkpoint choice, runtime, seed, variance, and parent configuration.
- Use paired-seed comparisons against the incumbent and report delta, standard error, confidence interval, and the exact acceptance criterion.
- Add a cheap screening stage using fewer epochs or a data subset, followed by confirmation only for promising candidates.
- Separate exploration validation from final model selection to limit adaptive validation overfitting.
- Make every accepted package trigger ablations so the scaffold learns which changes matter.
- Prefer warm starts, cached features, and shared negative samples where statistically valid.
- Avoid seed selection or “mean-logit seed close” unless it is a predeclared ensemble evaluated on an untouched split.

What the next run should try first

First, reproduce node 001 with multiple paired seeds to establish a trustworthy incumbent and uncertainty estimate. Then rerun node 002 as a single controlled change: replace pointwise BCE with complete-slate user-centered BCE while keeping every other setting, seed, split, and sample order fixed. It had the best nominal result and is cheaper and more interpretable than the sequence package.

If that paired effect is not reliable, test node 003 next under the same protocol. In parallel, ablate node 001’s additions—especially recency weighting, BPR mixing, and DCN capacity—to identify the smallest package that preserves the gain. Do not revisit the full Sequence DeepFM package until simpler loss and sampling changes have been resolved and the runtime budget supports proper replication.
